paragraphs.title: Drowning, Persecution, and Acknowledgment of Guilt

easy.explanation: He describes sinking in deep mire and deep waters where the floods overflow him.
easy.q: What images does the psalmist use to describe his distress?

easy.explanation: He begins by crying, “Save me, O God.”
easy.q: To whom does the psalmist cry for deliverance?

answers: They hate and persecute him without a cause
easy.explanation: He says those who hate him without a cause are more than the hairs of his head.
easy.q: How does the psalmist describe his enemies?

answers: The waters are deep and the mire causes him to sink
He is trapped inside a house
medium.explanation: He is in deep mire where there is no standing and in deep waters.
medium.q: Why is the psalmist unable to stand?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes mud that threatens to hold him fast and make him sink.
medium.q: What does “deep mire” suggest in this passage?

answers: They are more than the hairs of his head
Only one man is pursuing him
medium.explanation: He says those who hate him are more than the hairs of his head.
medium.q: How great is the number of his enemies?

answers: He suffers unjust persecution while acknowledging his own guilt
He is angry with every member of his family
challenge.explanation: He says his enemies persecute him without cause, yet he also admits that God knows his foolishness and sins.
challenge.q: What is the central tension in the psalmist’s words through verse 6?

answers: That his distress is continual and overwhelming
That he is taking a sea voyage
challenge.explanation: The mire, floods, deep waters, and overflowing waters portray danger surrounding him.
challenge.q: What does the repeated use of water imagery emphasize?

answers: He does not hide his moral condition from God
challenge.explanation: The psalmist openly acknowledges that God knows his foolishness and sins.
challenge.q: What does the statement “my sins are not hid from thee” show?

paragraphs.title: Disgrace, Isolation, and Zeal for God

answers: Those who wait on and seek God to be ashamed
easy.explanation: He asks that those who wait on and seek God not be ashamed or confounded for his sake.
easy.q: What does the psalmist fear his reproach will cause?

answers: He has become a stranger to his brethren and an alien to his mother’s children
He invites them to a feast
easy.explanation: He says he has become a stranger to his brethren and an alien to his mother’s children.
easy.q: How does the psalmist describe his relationship with his family?

easy.explanation: He says, “I made sackcloth also my garment.”
easy.q: What did the psalmist make his garment?

answers: His zeal for God’s house and his identification with God
medium.explanation: He says, “For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up,” and that the reproaches against God fell upon him.
medium.q: What does the psalmist connect with the reproach he has suffered?

medium.explanation: In this context, shame means public disgrace or humiliation.
medium.q: What does “shame” mean in the phrase “shame hath covered my face”?

answers: They made him a proverb and spoke against him
medium.explanation: Those at the gate spoke against him, and he became the song of the drunkards.
medium.q: How did people respond to the psalmist’s mourning?

answers: He fears that his disgrace will bring shame upon fellow believers
He is announcing that he has left his faith
challenge.explanation: He asks that his personal reproach not cause those who seek God to be ashamed or confounded.
challenge.q: Why does the psalmist mention those who wait on and seek God before describing his isolation?

answers: They describe his mourning and the public response to it
They concern the building of cities
challenge.explanation: Fasting and sackcloth express his sorrow, while mockery shows how the public treated him.
challenge.q: What is the relationship among fasting, sackcloth, and mockery in this passage?

answers: He sees the hostility against him as connected with hostility toward God
He denies any relationship with God
challenge.explanation: The psalmist understands the insults directed against God as also falling upon him because of his devotion to God.
challenge.q: What does “the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me” imply?

paragraphs.title: A Plea for Deliverance and Uncomforted Pain

answers: The mire, deep waters, and those who hate him
easy.explanation: He asks to be delivered from the mire, the deep waters, and his enemies.
easy.q: From what does the psalmist ask to be delivered?

easy.explanation: He asks God to hear him according to the truth of His salvation.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do in an acceptable time?

answers: His heart is broken and he finds no comforters
easy.explanation: He says reproach has broken his heart and that he found no comforters.
easy.q: What is the psalmist’s emotional condition?

answers: He is in trouble and needs a speedy answer
He is asking for a meal
medium.explanation: He says, “For I am in trouble: hear me speedily.”
medium.q: Why does the psalmist ask God not to hide His face?

medium.explanation: The deep is the threatening depth of water that could swallow him.
medium.q: What does “the deep” represent in “let not the deep swallow me up”?

answers: It moves from rescue from water and enemies to a request for God’s nearness and answer
It moves from thanksgiving to cursing
It moves from a feast to fasting
medium.explanation: He asks for rescue, then for God to hear him, draw near, redeem him, and deliver him.
medium.q: How does the plea for deliverance develop in these verses?

answers: Danger from every side and the absence of escape
A journey to a new city
challenge.explanation: Together they picture drowning, being swallowed, and being shut in without escape.
challenge.q: What do the images of water, the pit, and the deep emphasize together?

answers: Having no human comforters, he seeks God’s nearness
His broken heart makes him stop praying
challenge.explanation: Because he finds no pity or comfort, he asks God to draw near and redeem him.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the psalmist’s broken heart and his prayer?

answers: They gave him vinegar to drink
They hid the pit from him
challenge.explanation: The verse says, “in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”
challenge.q: What cruel treatment did the psalmist receive when he was thirsty?

paragraphs.title: The Curse on the Enemies and the Plea for Judgment

answers: That it become a place of prayer
easy.explanation: He asks that their table become a snare and a trap.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask to happen to his enemies’ table?

answers: That they be darkened so they cannot see
That they close only at night
easy.explanation: He says, “Let their eyes be darkened, that they see not.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask to happen to his enemies’ eyes?

answers: That his enemies be blotted out of it
That they be written in it first
That it be kept by them
easy.explanation: He asks that they be blotted out of the book of the living and not written with the righteous.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask concerning the book of the living?

medium.explanation: He asks for darkened eyes, shaking loins, indignation, wrath, and desolate habitations.
medium.q: What punishments does the psalmist call down upon his enemies?

answers: Something intended to catch or hinder
medium.explanation: A trap is something that catches, ensnares, or causes someone to fall.
medium.q: What is a “trap” in the phrase “let it become a trap”?

answers: He asks that his enemies not be counted among the living and righteous
He asks that they receive honor
It concerns the construction of tents
medium.explanation: He asks that they not remain in the book of the living or be written with the righteous.
medium.q: How does the request to be blotted out of the book relate to the psalmist’s plea for judgment?

answers: A place intended for welfare and food becomes a snare for the enemies
The table disappears from the psalm
challenge.explanation: That which should have been for their welfare is turned into a trap.
challenge.q: What makes the table a symbol of judgment?

answers: The psalmist asks for judgment upon those who persecuted and wounded the afflicted
He admits that they never harmed anyone
He asks for a reward for them
challenge.explanation: He describes enemies who persecute the smitten and add grief to the wounded, then asks God to judge them.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the enemies’ persecution and the judgment requested?

answers: Verse 29 ends the plea for judgment, while the next section turns toward salvation and praise
Verse 29 contains thanksgiving, followed by a curse
challenge.explanation: After asking for judgment, the psalmist turns to God’s salvation, praise, and thanksgiving.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between verse 29 and the following verses?

paragraphs.title: Salvation, Thanksgiving, and Hope for Zion

answers: Praise God’s name with a song and thanksgiving
easy.explanation: He says, “I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving.”
easy.q: What will the psalmist do after God’s salvation?

answers: Those who sit at the gate only
easy.explanation: The verse says, “The humble shall see this, and be glad.”
easy.q: Who will be glad when they see what God has done?

answers: Save Zion and build the cities of Judah
easy.explanation: The psalm says God will save Zion and build the cities of Judah.
easy.q: What will God do for Zion and the cities of Judah?

answers: The psalmist emphasizes praise and thanksgiving as pleasing worship
There is no prayer in the psalm
medium.explanation: He says praising God with thanksgiving pleases the LORD better than an ox or bullock.
medium.q: Why is thanksgiving better pleasing to the LORD than an ox or bullock?

answers: It is an animal with horns and divided hoofs
It is an animal with wings
It is an animal with fins
medium.explanation: The phrase describes a horned animal with hoofs, such as an ox or bullock.
medium.q: What does “horns and hoofs” indicate about the bullock?

answers: From the psalmist to the humble, the poor, and all creation
From the enemies to the wilderness only
From the city to the psalmist only
medium.explanation: Praise extends from the individual to the humble, the poor, heaven, earth, the seas, and every living thing.
medium.q: How does the circle of praise expand near the end of the psalm?

answers: His deliverance encourages and strengthens those who seek God
His salvation separates him from them
challenge.explanation: The humble rejoice, and those who seek God are encouraged: “your heart shall live.”
challenge.q: What is the connection between the psalmist’s salvation and the joy of the humble?

answers: God does not despise the afflicted and imprisoned
God turns away from the needy
challenge.explanation: The verse declares that the LORD hears the poor and does not despise His prisoners.
challenge.q: What does “the LORD heareth the poor” emphasize about God?

answers: A movement from personal distress to praise, salvation, rebuilding, and dwelling
challenge.explanation: The conclusion moves from poverty and sorrow to praise, encouragement, cosmic worship, and the restoration of Zion and Judah.
challenge.q: What overall picture emerges from the end of the psalm?
